d.title: A refusal the model can relay, not a stack trace
d.caption: **The tool body never printed, which is the only proof that a block really blocked.** What the model received was the callback's dict presented as an ordinary function response, so it relayed the reason in its own words and the refusal reached the user as a sentence. **Raising instead produces the two bad agents:** one that apologises vaguely, and one that retries the same call. The `retryable: False` key is the convention worth adopting — it tells the model to stop asking.

d.title: Zero model calls, and what the saving actually was
d.caption: **The counter is the measurement: a subclass incrementing on every `generate_content_async` reported zero.** Returning an `LlmResponse` from `before_model_callback` short-circuits the call, which is the shape of both an input guardrail and a cache — check, and if you already know the answer, return it. **The saving is larger than it looks**, because the request never sent was the whole assembled conversation, not one message. **And the trap is in the last row:** a keyword check stops one phrasing and refuses innocent mentions; the mechanism is right, the policy is not.

d.title: Callback, plugin, tool or instruction
d.caption: **Two questions settle it.** Must this happen whether the model wants it to or not? If yes it is a control, and the only remaining question is scope — one agent's policy is a callback, every agent's is a plugin. If the model should be able to *choose* it, it is a capability, and capabilities are tools. **The branch to avoid is the fourth one:** policy written into the instruction and hoped for. An instruction is a request; a callback is a control, and the difference only shows up on the day it matters.

d.title: Six plugins worth having, and which hook each one needs
d.caption: **Note where the global guardrail sits:** `on_user_message` runs before any agent does, so it cannot be bypassed by a transfer to a specialist whose own callbacks you forgot to wire. That is the property a per-agent callback cannot give you. **And `google.adk.plugins` exports `BasePlugin` and `PluginManager` and nothing else** — every row here is yours to write, which is a small amount of work for your fields, your log line and your sink.

d.title: Why the start time is popped on both paths
d.caption: **A dictionary that only ever grows is a memory leak in a long-running service**, and the error path is exactly where it grows: a turn that raises never reaches `after_run`, so its entry stays forever. Popping in `on_run_error` too is the whole fix. **The bigger argument is the third agent:** add one to the pipeline and it appears in the log with no edit, where the callback equivalent is a line of registration per agent that a reviewer will not notice is missing — because nothing fails when a logging callback is absent. **Silence is the worst failure mode for observability.**

d.title: Three design decisions, readable straight off the signatures
d.caption: **An artifact is a `types.Part` — the same object a model message is made of** — so a saved chart or document can be handed back to the model without conversion. `save_artifact` returning an `int` means versions are assigned by the service rather than by your filenames, so saving the same name three times gives you three versions rather than one overwrite. **And `session_id` being optional everywhere is the whole namespace design:** pass it and the file belongs to this conversation, omit it and it belongs to the user.

d.title: Artifacts, your own storage, or neither
d.caption: **The question to ask is who else needs this file, and for how long.** A chart the agent just rendered is the conversation's, and artifacts give it versioning and a tie to the event log for free. An invoice your finance system owns has a lifecycle of its own — write it to your storage and keep the URL in state. **And the omission to avoid is at the bottom:** the runner takes `artifact_service` exactly as it takes `session_service`, and without one `save_artifact` has nowhere to go. Wire it in alongside the session service, not when the first tool needs it.

d.title: Every field description is sent to the provider as prompt
d.caption: **That is what makes the schema the natural home for the rules that used to clutter the instruction.** `Field(description="ISO 4217 code, uppercase")` beats a sentence in the prompt saying the same thing, because it sits next to the field it governs and cannot drift from it. **So write schemas the way you would write a good API contract:** the class docstring says what the object is, each description says what the field means and what form it takes — and what remains in the instruction is the task rather than the format.

d.title: A classifier the pipeline can branch on without a model call
d.caption: **The payoff is in the last row: a typed object in state means the next step routes in Python rather than by asking a model.** A classifier that returns a paragraph forces the next step to re-read it; one that returns a category, an urgency and a boolean lets your own code decide. **`Literal` is the field to insist on** — it becomes an enum the provider enforces, where a plain string with an instruction saying “one of three” eventually produces `Billing`, `tech` and something you have never seen, each breaking a dictionary lookup differently.
